Also, the paragraph about Generic_City and the cooking class doesn't clearly return to your main argument about activity and inactivity. Try opening each paragraph with a sentence that links to your thesis, and use a clearer transition to show how your examples support your position.

You use a range of sentence types, including complex sentences with subordinate clauses, such as "if you fill your time with friends and activities that you like to do, you will not feel want to be alone." Some sentences become hard to follow because they are very long or join several ideas with "and." The sentence about your swimming coach is especially tangled. Breaking long sentences into two shorter ones would make your meaning clearer.

You choose some effective, specific words, such as "push" and "achieve" to describe effort and goals. Some word choices are vague or not quite right for the meaning you intend. "Bad community" and "stuff" are informal or unclear, and "the succeed person" uses a word that doesn't quite fit. More precise vocabulary, such as a specific term for the skills you mention in the cooking class, would strengthen your writing.

You use some useful collocations and fixed expressions, such as "feed their families," "stay active and social with others," and "a bad time." Some common phrases are not used in their standard form, which may confuse readers. For example, "a good friends all over you" should be "good friends" with a different structure, and "a time alone" could be phrased as "time alone" or "being alone." Learning the standard forms of common expressions will make your writing sound more natural.

Your writing shows control of many structures, such as the use of "will" for future meaning and "have to" for obligation. There are several errors in agreement, word form, and tense. "Succeed" should be "successful" or "successful person" in this context, "an old friends" needs singular agreement, "Other's" should be "Others" (no apostrophe), and "a good friends" also needs correcting. Some verb forms are also incorrect, such as "feel want" and "vising" (visiting). Also, "seasoning the food" would be more accurate as "seasoning" or "season the food." Rereading each sentence for these forms will help.

Your essay is mostly readable, and you use capital letters at the start of sentences. There are several errors to address. "Other's" should be "Others," "their" should be "there" in "in their," "vising" should be "visiting," and "self" should be "myself" as one word. "Olympic Golden medal" should use lowercase for "golden." A comma after "Another reason" is also unnecessary. Proofreading specifically for these spelling, punctuation, and capitalization errors will improve your score.

studentFacing: You use a good range of linking words and phrases, such as "Still," "However," "In fact," "Moreover," and "Therefore," which help guide the reader. Some references are vague, though. "This fact shows" and "This fact proves" do not clearly point back to a specific idea, so name the fact each time. Phrases like "This is an important issue" are repeated across paragraphs, so vary them or cut them. Also, your opening anecdote does not clearly connect to your argument about curfews. A sentence linking the story to the thesis would help.

You write a mix of simple and compound sentences, and you sometimes use subordinate clauses such as "because" and "which." To build on this, try adding more varied structures, such as sentences that open with a subordinate clause or use participial phrases. Some sentences become hard to follow, and a few have faulty parallelism or tangled clauses. Check that the items in a list or contrast share the same grammatical form, and break long sentences into shorter ones where needed.

You use some precise and effective words, such as "anxious," "unfairly interfere," and "vicious." Some word choices are imprecise or incorrect in context, though. "Molarity" appears to be a mistake for "morality," and "threat" should be the verb "threaten." You also use "unfortunate" many times, so look for more specific alternatives such as "harmful," "tragic," or "serious." Checking a dictionary for word forms and meanings will help you choose words more precisely.

You use some strong fixed expressions, such as "keep teenagers out of trouble," "for the rest of their lives," and "stay out of any trouble." Some common collocations and prepositions need correction. For example, "pay attention to" is the standard form, "put an end to" is used rather than "put an end on," and "get into trouble" is more natural than "get trouble." Learning frequent expressions as whole chunks will help you sound more natural.

You generally control tense and sentence basics, but several errors recur. Use "an idea" or "a thought" rather than "a thinking," and match verbs to singular or plural subjects ("the curfews is" should be "the curfews are" or "the curfew is"). Use base forms after modal verbs and "to" ("should be publish" and "should be obey" should be "should be published" and "should obey"). Use the correct word form, such as "moral" as a noun versus "morality," and "robbers appearing" rather than "appear." Watch for the "-ing" and past participle forms after "had" and "will."

Your ideas are easy to follow, but there are several spelling and punctuation errors to correct. Check spelling carefully, since words such as "Lucikly," "Unfortuantely," "consequense," and "carrried" are misspelled. Use an apostrophe correctly in possessives ("teenagers' future" and not "teenagers's"). Capitalize proper nouns and abbreviations consistently ("U.S. government"), and use title case consistently in the title, where minor words such as "of" are usually lowercase. Proofread for these patterns before you submit.

studentFacing: Your essay is organised around the three reasons, and signposts like "First of all", "Another reason is" and "Last reason why" help the reader follow the structure. Some connections are unclear, though. The sentence "Because, they are not financially good with money" does not clearly link to the point before it, and the last body paragraph repeats ideas instead of developing them. Clearer linking words and a more precise explanation of how each reason connects to the main claim would strengthen the flow.

Most of your sentences are simple or compound, which makes your ideas easy to follow. Try combining short sentences and controlling longer ones more carefully. The sentence beginning "If students need to help there families out" joins several clauses with "and" and no punctuation, so it becomes hard to read. Using a mix of sentence lengths and some subordinate clauses would show more control.

You communicate your ideas clearly, but your word choice is often general and repetitive. "Early" and "get over with" appear many times, and phrases like "keep on going to school" could be more precise. Using more specific words, such as "accelerate", "well-paid" or "obligation", would make your arguments more persuasive and varied.

You use some useful expressions, such as "help out" and "start making money", and these work well in context. Other combinations sound unnatural, such as "a good financial job", which is more naturally expressed as "a well-paid job" or "a stable career". Also, "get that over with" is informal for an argumentative essay. Learning standard collocations for academic writing would make your language sound more natural.

Your sentences are mostly understandable, but there are recurring errors. "There" is used where "their" is needed, several nouns and verbs do not agree, and the article "a" is used before a vowel sound. Check the agreement in "Some school district offer programs" and "these are three good reason", and use "their" for possession, "by themselves" for reflexive pronouns, and "them" as the object pronoun. Reviewing these points will improve your accuracy considerably.

Your ideas are readable, but spelling and punctuation need attention. Contractions are missing their apostrophes ("dont"), possessives are misused ("family's" and "students parents"), and some commas are placed incorrectly ("Because, they are"). Also, the spelling "there" for "their" appears often. Proofreading for these specific points would make your writing look more polished.

The essay uses clear signposting for its three reasons and a conclusion, which gives it a visible structure. Cohesion weakens where pronouns and references are unclear, such as 'they' in the sentence about the students' parents and families.
Most sentences are simple or compound, joined with 'and' and 'so'. One long sentence strings several clauses together without punctuation, so the reader loses the logical relationships between them.
The phrase 'at a early age' is repeated many times in place of more varied wording, which limits the range of word choice and reduces precision.
The essay uses a few common expressions, such as 'get over with', but most collocations are basic or unidiomatic, for example 'live be them self' and 'financially good with money'.

Subject-verb and noun-number agreement is inconsistent: 'these are three good reason' uses a singular noun after a plural number, and the possessive plural is mismatched in 'The students parents may work but they need that extra help for their kid.'

Spelling and punctuation errors occur throughout, including the missing apostrophe in possessives, the misuse of 'there' for 'their', a comma between 'Because' and its clause, and the contraction 'dont' without an apostrophe.

Adding a sentence that links each example back to the main claim would also help.

You use a clear range of simple sentences, and you have started to use longer sentences with "if" clauses. Some of these longer sentences join several ideas with commas and "and" in ways that make them hard to follow. Try splitting them into shorter sentences, or use a clause structure like "If you hear that..., you can..." to keep the main action clear.

You use clear everyday words that communicate your ideas. The vocabulary is quite repetitive, with "new" and "fun" appearing often. Try replacing some of these with more precise words, such as "engaging," "rewarding," or "worthwhile," to show a wider range.

You use some useful expressions, such as "participate in school activities" and "learn from the experiences of others." Phrases like "experience the fun time" sound unnatural, though, and you could use more natural collocations such as "have a great time" or "take part in." Expanding your range of set phrases will make your writing sound more fluent.

Most of your verb forms are correct, and your sentences generally agree. Some errors need attention. "Informations" is an uncountable noun and does not take a plural form. Also, "participated on" should be "participated in." Checking these forms will improve your accuracy.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but there are several spelling errors, including "learm," "intrested," and "informations." There is also a stray space before a comma and a missing full stop after the opening line. Proofreading for spelling and punctuation will make your writing more polished.

studentFacing: The essay uses signposts ('My first reason', 'My last reason') but has no middle reason, so the sequence of ideas is incomplete. The conclusion also restates the introduction nearly word for word, which weakens the flow between paragraphs.

Sentences are mostly simple or compound, with one conditional opening ('If you hear...') that is undermined by a long, loosely joined clause. The clause mixes a sentence-final comma and a shift in structure, which limits control of complex structures.
Vocabulary is mostly basic and repetitive. The phrase 'learn new information' and similar wording recur, with few precise or varied word choices beyond 'experience' and 'benefits'.

Some collocations are non-standard, such as 'participated on a school activity', where 'in' is the expected preposition. Otherwise the writer uses common fixed expressions such as 'try new things' and 'not going to regret it' appropriately.

There are word-form and agreement errors, including the uncountable-style plural 'informations' and a tense/number mismatch between 'participated' and 'keeps talking' in the same sentence. The opening is also a sentence fragment.

Your ideas connect well overall. The transitions 'Therefore,' and 'Finally,' signal your logical moves, and each paragraph has a clear focus. To strengthen cohesion further, use more varied linking words (such as 'For example,' 'However,' or 'In addition,') and make the links between your reasons and your conclusion more explicit. Your last sentence about others disagreeing also needs to connect back to the argument more clearly.

You use some complex sentences with subordinate clauses, such as 'as long as' and 'so that.' However, several sentences are very long and join ideas with 'because' and commas, which makes them hard to follow. Try breaking some long sentences into two shorter ones, and vary your sentence openings more.

Your word choice is generally clear, but you repeat 'good' many times, which limits your range. Replace some instances with more precise words, such as 'sound,' 'wise,' 'strong,' 'reliable,' or 'rewarding.' Also consider more academic terms like 'prerequisites' or 'long-term prospects' where they fit.

You use some useful collocations, such as 'committing to a career' and 'in case you decide.' Some expressions need correction: 'get a feel of' should be 'get a feel for,' and 'pursue in that career' should be 'pursue that career.' Learning fixed expressions like these will make your writing sound more natural.

Your sentences are mostly grammatical, but there are some errors. 'At young age' needs the article 'a,' 'pursue in that career' should drop 'in,' and the phrase 'about this career' is redundant after 'very passionate about this career' in a sentence that is already long. Also, a comma is placed between the subject and verb in 'most jobs, don't hire.'

Your punctuation and spelling need attention. 'Thats' needs an apostrophe ('That's') each time you use it. A new sentence should begin with a capital letter, and 'although' should be capitalised at the start of its sentence. Also, remove the comma between 'jobs' and 'don't' and check your commas around introductory phrases.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure. The signposts "First," "Socond," "Third," "Fourth," and "In conclusion" help the reader follow your reasons. To strengthen cohesion, check that each paragraph's point connects clearly to your thesis. For example, the link between a student being rejected and missing school is hard to follow. Also, add references such as "this," "these," or "such behaviour" so each sentence builds on the one before.

You use some longer sentences with subordinate clauses, such as the opening sentence with "Although." Several sentences, however, join separate ideas with only a comma or with "and," which makes them run on. Try splitting long sentences at natural points, or use connectors such as "because," "so," or "which" to show how ideas relate. Varying sentence length and structure will also make your writing easier to read.

You choose a clear, relevant range of topic words, such as "cheating," "attention," and "confidence." Some word choices are imprecise or incorrect in context, though. For example, "trouble" is used as a verb in places where "cause trouble" or "disrupt" would fit, and "disturb" is used as an adjective where "disruptive" is needed. Using more precise vocabulary will help your argument sound more academic and convincing.

You use some useful expressions, such as "got a good grade" and "make bad for the other students." Some common collocations need correction. For example, students "take" a test rather than "do" a test, and you can say "cause trouble" or "disrupt the class" instead of "makes trouble." Learning fixed phrases such as "pay attention" and "cheat on a test" will make your English sound more natural.

You generally communicate your ideas clearly, but there are recurring problems with verb forms and agreement. Watch for mixed tenses and missing or incorrect verb forms, such as "listing" for "listening" and "doing" without a helping verb. Also check subject-verb agreement, as in "one students" and "Their is." Checking each sentence for these patterns will improve accuracy considerably.

Your ideas are understandable, but spelling and punctuation errors appear often and sometimes affect clarity. Examples include "Socond," "Their is," "internate acsses," and "kownleage." Also, there are errors such as an extra comma after "because" and a space before a full stop. Use spell-check and proofread for these patterns. Be consistent in spelling "cell phone" or "cellphone" throughout. Also, check whether each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with the correct punctuation.

studentFacing: You use some useful linking phrases, such as "Thanks to" and "With all this being said," and each paragraph has a clear focus. The first paragraph jumps between topics, though. The landscaping experience appears before you have introduced it, so the reader loses the thread. Introducing each new idea in its own paragraph, or previewing it in the opening, would help the essay flow.

Most of your sentences are short and simple, which makes the letter easy to follow. Try combining some of them with subordinate clauses or conjunctions to show more range. Some sentences need fixing: a comma is used where a full stop or a conjunction is needed, and one sentence is missing its main verb.

You choose clear, appropriate words for your experiences, such as "patient," "confident," and "organized." To make your vocabulary more precise, replace general verbs like "gain" and "help" with more specific choices. For example, you could say you "developed" a skill or "assisted" customers.

You use some useful expressions, such as "under a lot of pressure" and "take your time." Some word combinations do not sound natural in English. "Peer pressure" usually means pressure from classmates or friends, not from a family member, so "during peer pressure" does not quite fit. "Use to" should be "used to." Learning these fixed combinations will make your writing sound more natural.

Your writing is generally understandable, but there are recurring problems with verb forms and subject-verb agreement. Use "has helped" (not "has help") and "these classes have" (not "This classes have"). Use "would like" instead of "will like" when making polite requests. Also check the tense in "I learn" when you are describing past events.

Your ideas come through clearly, but spelling, capitalisation and punctuation errors appear often. Check common words such as "customers," "opportunities," "planning," and "that's." Use the apostrophe in "I'm" and write "McDonald's" as one word. Capitalise "Auto Tech" consistently and use "a" before "Auto" in "an Auto technician" if you keep the phrase. Proofreading for these points would make a big difference.

studentFacing: You use a good range of linking words and phrases, such as "Firstable,", "Also,", "On the other hand," and "Consequently,", which help the reader follow your structure. Some connections are unclear, though. In your second body paragraph, "For examples" introduces a point that doesn't clearly follow from the idea before it, and in the first paragraph the link between the girl's story and your claim is left implicit. Also, the referent of "that" is often unclear, so consider naming the idea directly to make each link explicit.

You attempt a variety of structures, including subordinate clauses and sentences that begin with linking adverbials. Several sentences, however, are long and tangled, with multiple clauses joined by commas where the grammatical relationship between them is hard to follow. Breaking some of these into shorter, clearer sentences, or using subordination more deliberately, would give you better control of your sentence structure.

You have a reasonable base of topic vocabulary, such as "online," "video conferencing," "communicate" and "environment." To improve precision, look for more exact words. For example, "advantegious" is a word you are trying to reach for, and "understable" would be better expressed as "understandable" or, more precisely, "easier to understand." Choosing more specific verbs and adjectives in place of general ones such as "more" would also strengthen your expression.

You use some useful expressions, such as "hold one point of view" and "give up to study alone." Some collocations need adjusting, however. "Catch up" is usually followed by "on" or "with" (for example, "catch up on late work"), and "give up" is normally followed by a verb in the -ing form ("give up studying alone"). Practising these fixed phrases will make your writing sound more natural.

Your writing communicates your ideas, but there are recurring problems with agreement, verb forms and word forms. Examples include the verb form after "could" and "can't", the subject-verb agreement in "she have", and the use of "every" with a plural noun. Also, the word "impact" is used as a verb without the correct form. Reviewing these patterns will help your sentences become more accurate.

Your essay has several spelling errors and inconsistent punctuation and capitalisation. Words such as "Firstable," "thier," "behaivior" and "studehts" need correcting. The pronoun "I" should be capitalised in all positions, and sentences should not start with a capital letter after a comma. Careful proofreading, especially of commonly misspelt words, will make a clear difference to how your writing is received.

The essay's stated position is contradictory: the opening says online attendance would not benefit students, while the conclusion says students would benefit, though not all of them. The writer does not explain how the body paragraphs lead to this change.

Some transitions work well, such as "After all" and "In conclusion." Adding more connecting words between sentences within paragraphs would make the links between your ideas clearer. Also, "Its best that you seek help" follows a warning, so consider a linking phrase that shows how the advice follows from the example.

You use a mix of simple and complex sentences, and some longer sentences with subordinate clauses show good control. Several sentences are very long and join many ideas with "and" or "that," which can make the meaning harder to follow. Breaking some of these into two shorter sentences would help readers. Varying your sentence openings would also add variety.

You choose appropriate general words such as "downfall," "expert," and "circumstance" to discuss the topic. Some words are used loosely or repeated ("good," "things," "life"). Using more precise words, such as "qualified" or "counselling," and varying repeated terms would make your ideas sharper.

You use some useful expressions, such as "deal with a lot of issues," "fall apart," and "make the right decisions," which sound natural. Some phrases are unnatural, such as "go for to seek for guidance," where "seek" and "go for" are unnecessary. Learning standard collocations like "seek guidance" or "go for counselling" would improve your naturalness.

Your sentences are mostly understandable, but there are several errors in word forms, verb use, and agreement. Examples include "this days" (should be "these days"), "their's no age limit," and "easier that" (should be "than"). Also, "the do not know" needs a verb ("they do not know"). Checking these structures carefully will help your accuracy.

Your work contains frequent errors in punctuation, spacing, and apostrophes. "Its" should be "It's" when it means "it is," "you're" is used where "your" is needed, and there are missing spaces after commas and before full stops. A semicolon is also used incorrectly before "meaning." Proofreading specifically for apostrophes and spacing would make a clear difference.

studentFacing: You signal your structure clearly with transitions such as 'One reason', 'Another reason why' and 'Finally', which helps the reader follow your argument. The link between your examples and your claim could be stronger. The Einstein, Musk and Jobs examples are listed one after another, and the sentence 'It's all in the head, that's where it all starts from' does not explicitly tie them back to the idea that imagination comes before knowledge. Try a sentence at the end of each example that states what it proves, and consider linking your final paragraph back to your opening analogy.

Most of your sentences are simple or compound, such as 'Imagination is alot more important than you think it is.' You do use some longer structures, for example 'Just constant knowledge is boring, but adding imagination is like adding sprinkles on to a boring vanilla cake.' Adding more complex sentences, such as ones with subordinate clauses introduced by 'because', 'although' or 'which', would show more control over sentence structure and make your reasoning more precise.

You use some effective, topic-appropriate words, such as 'unthinkable', 'innovative' and 'fuels the mind'. 'Imagination' is repeated very often, and general words such as 'cool', 'good' and 'things' appear in places where more precise language would work better. For example, 'cool things' could name the specific benefits you mean, such as creativity, problem-solving or emotional resilience. Replacing some repeated words with synonyms or more exact terms would widen your range.

You use some useful collocations and expressions, such as 'come up with', 'in many ways' and 'pretty often'. Some phrases sound unnatural, though, such as 'imagined in it all in his head', which would read more naturally as 'imagined it all in his head'. Phrases like 'in many ways' and 'in different ways' are used repeatedly, so a wider set of connecting expressions would sound more fluent.

Your writing shows good control of tense in most places. There are several errors to fix. 'How you think Elon Musk' needs the auxiliary 'do' to form a question. 'a mind filled of knowledge' should be 'filled with knowledge'. 'a better by work outing' should be 'a better person by working out'. In 'making you a better person or be a more fun person', the second verb should match the first, so 'or to be' is needed. 'work outing' should be 'working out' and 'going on jogs' is a valid form.

Your punctuation is mostly accurate, and you use a comma after the introductory phrase 'Quantum physicist'. There are several spelling and punctuation errors to correct. 'alot' should be 'a lot' in both places it appears. 'on to' should be 'onto'. The sentence 'Quantum physicist, Albert Einstein once said' would benefit from a comma after 'said' before the quotation, as in 'Einstein once said: "Imagination..."'. Add commas after introductory phrases such as 'For example' and 'As a result'.

The essay has a clear structure: an introduction, three body paragraphs each opening with a signposted reason, and a conclusion. Transitions such as 'One reason why', 'Another reason' and 'Finally' make the organisation easy to follow.
Most sentences are simple or compound. There is some control of longer structures, such as the opening conditional sentence, but the essay shows little variety in sentence openings and structures.
Word choice is mostly general and repetitive (e.g. 'cool', 'fun', 'boring'). Some more precise vocabulary appears, such as 'unthinkable' and 'fuels', but it is used sparingly.
There is a spelling error: 'alot' should be 'a lot'. Otherwise capitalisation and punctuation in the essay are generally accurate, including the quotation and the proper nouns.

studentFacing: Your ideas follow a logical order and you use some useful linking words, such as "because", "For example" and "So". To improve, divide your essay into separate paragraphs, for example one for your opinion, one or two for reasons with examples, and one for your conclusion. Use a wider range of linkers, such as "however", "as a result" or "in addition", to show how each idea connects to the last. Also try to avoid repeating "failure" and "why" so often, and use pronouns and synonyms to refer back to ideas.

You use simple, compound and some complex sentences, such as "without failure we may not know how to be thankful for it if we pass in the first place". This shows you can build longer sentences. To make your writing more controlled, try to vary your sentence openings, avoid long chains of clauses joined by "and" or "but", and check that each sentence has a clear main clause. Breaking up very long sentences would make your ideas easier to follow.

You use some good topic words, such as "thankful", "unsuccessful" and "pursuit of success", and you explain your ideas with simple, clear language. Some word choices are not quite right, though. For example, "rule" should be "role" in "the important rule of the pursuit of success", and "bigger" in "Our brains get's bigger" does not fully express your meaning. Try learning more precise words for ideas such as learning, improvement and persistence, and check that each word fits the context.

You use some useful expressions, such as "the end of the world" and "make it right", which sound natural in this context. To develop this further, learn more common collocations and fixed phrases, such as "learn from mistakes", "a valuable lesson", "keep trying" or "set a goal". Using these would make your argument sound more fluent and natural.

Your essay contains several grammar errors that sometimes make the meaning unclear. Examples include the verb form "tell" in "failure tell us", the verb in "what did everyting went wrong", "Our brains get's bigger" (the verb should agree with the plural subject and have no apostrophe), and "it dosen't mean" (the auxiliary is "doesn't"). Your sentences with "the more we fail the more we know" show that you can use comparative structures correctly, so build on that. Review subject-verb agreement, the use of auxiliary verbs in questions and negatives, and past tense forms.

Your essay has several spelling, capitalisation and punctuation errors. Examples include "everyting", "faliure", "dosen't", "get's", the lowercase "i" in "i agree" and "i mean", and the space before commas and question marks ("failure ,because", "this ?"). Your use of apostrophes in "Churchill's" and "it's" is correct. Proofread for spelling, always capitalise "I", and check that apostrophes and punctuation marks are placed correctly. A quick spell-check and a careful final read would help a lot.

studentFacing: You use clear signposting to organise the essay, with transitions such as "For starters," "In addition," "Furthermore," and "And finally." Your paragraphs follow a logical order. To strengthen cohesion, check that each transition matches the idea that follows it. "Furthermore" introduces a point about losing imagination, which is a contrast with the earlier argument, so a transition like "On the other hand" or "Without it" might fit better. Also keep one consistent reference point: you shift between "it," "you," "they," and "his or hers" in the same paragraph, which can make it unclear who or what you mean.

You use a mix of simple and compound sentences, which makes your ideas easy to follow. Several sentences begin with "Because," however, and these are incomplete as written. Try joining them to the sentence before, or rewrite them as complete clauses. Using a wider range of structures, such as subordinate clauses with "although" or "when," would also show more control. Some sentences are long and tangled, so breaking them up would help, for example in the sentence about the "specificly just of types" of science studies.

You have chosen some useful content words, such as "invent," "benefit," and "accomplish," and you use the key term "imagination" consistently. Some word choices are imprecise or misspelled, and this reduces clarity. For example, "veritile" should be "versatile," and "a important key" would be clearer as "an important key." The phrase "humble life" is also used in a way that does not quite match the meaning you seem to intend. Choosing more precise words such as "versatile," "contribute," or "fulfil" would give your argument more impact.

You use some useful expressions, such as "sum it all up" and "in order to," which give the essay a natural, academic tone. Some common collocations are not yet fully established. For example, "the life that your planning" should be "the life that you are planning," and "call your future doomed" is not a standard phrase. Learning fixed collocations such as "plan for the future," "make a difference," and "tackle social problems" would help your writing sound more natural.

Your writing shows good control of basic sentence meaning, but there are recurring errors with agreement, articles, and word forms. Use "an" before vowel sounds, as in "an engineer" and "an author." Use "a" before consonant sounds, as in "a sergeant." Check word forms too: "Politician wise" and "Mathematic wise" need the correct noun or adjective form, and "your future no might be" needs "not" and a clear verb structure. Also check that "I" is always capitalised and that verbs agree with their subjects.

Your spelling needs careful proofreading, since many words are misspelled, including "benifit," "sociaty," "finnetial," "mathimatical," "jornalism," and "sientist." Capitalise proper nouns and the pronoun "I": "Albert Einstein" needs capitals and the correct spelling, and "i" should be "I." Capitalise the first word of each sentence and any adjective or noun derived from a proper noun, such as "Politician" when used as the start of a phrase. Also check that commas separate clauses correctly, for example after introductory phrases.

You use a mix of simple and compound sentences, which gives your writing some variety. Some sentences join two independent clauses with only a comma, which makes them hard to follow. For example, 'Students get in trouble because of the cell phone, they don't think before they use the phone' could be split into two sentences.

You use clear everyday words such as 'wasting their time' and 'get in trouble', which communicate your message. To make your argument more precise and persuasive, try more specific academic words in place of general ones, such as 'distraction' instead of 'things other than the classwork' or 'consequences' instead of 'the risk that they might get into'.

You use some useful expressions, such as 'get in trouble' and 'wasting their time'. Some phrases sound unnatural, though. 'Finish as much as I can of work' is more natural as 'finish as much work as I can', and the phrase 'use it wisely' is the standard collocation for what you mean.

'Stricts' should be 'strict', and 'I saw students were watching' should be 'I saw students watching' or 'I saw that students were watching'.

studentFacing: Your ideas mostly follow a clear sequence, and the examples (the teacher and the missing book, the staying-after-school scenario) help the reader follow your points. The connectors need work, though. "Therefore" signals a conclusion, but the sentences it introduces do not follow logically from the previous ones. Try words like "Also," "As a result," or "For example," depending on the relationship you mean.

You use a mix of simple and compound sentences, which makes your writing readable. Most sentences follow similar patterns, though, and a few long sentences join several clauses with "but" or commas, which can make them hard to follow. Try varying your openings, using some complex sentences with subordinate clauses (for example, "Although some parents..."), and breaking up the longest sentences.

You use some relevant words, such as "connected" and "alerts," but several word choices are general or vague ("things," "much power," "something"). Replacing these with more precise terms, such as "resources," "capability," or a specific example, would make your ideas clearer and more persuasive.

Some expressions are not idiomatic in English. "In an easy matter" should be "with ease" or "easily," and "in any device" should be "on any device." The opening image, "sweet time on the palm for your hands," is also unclear as a figurative phrase. Learning common collocations, such as "stay connected with," "keep up with," and "on any device," will help your writing sound more natural.

There are several errors with word forms, agreement, and tense. Examples include "parent" (should be "parents"), "other" (should be "others"), "miss" (should be "missing" after "like"), and a shift from past to present in the hypothetical sentence ("If they did, they can type" should be "they could type"). Also, "much power" should be "a lot of power" or "great power" with a countable or uncountable noun. Reviewing these patterns will improve accuracy.

Punctuation and spelling need attention. Question marks should not be combined with periods, a comma is missing after "relieved" and a space after it, and "Some teaches" should be "Some teachers." Sentences should also start with capital letters, as in "alerts will pop up." Commas around introductory and parenthetical phrases, such as "Technology, also allows," should be checked as well.

Also check where you place commas, since the sentence about commitment is hard to parse.

Some word choices are not quite accurate, such as "make impossible" (where a verb like "make it harder" or "stop" might fit better) and "sacrifices" used as a verb. However, the paragraphs are connected mainly by repetition rather than by transitions that show how each idea relates to the argument. Adding linking phrases (for example, 'Furthermore' or 'In contrast') and tying the final paragraph back to your opening claim would strengthen the flow. Pronoun use also shifts between 'the person', 'it', and 'they', so keeping one consistent reference would help the reader follow.

You use a variety of sentence openings, such as 'Being able to...' and 'Not letting people...', which is a good start. Several sentences, though, join separate ideas without punctuation or connectors, which makes them hard to follow. Breaking these into shorter sentences or linking them with clear conjunctions would give you more control over your sentence structures.

You use some effective academic words, such as 'originality', 'isolate', and 'capability', which add precision to your ideas. You also rely on the same phrase several times, such as 'a big', which narrows your range. Choosing more specific alternatives (for example, 'significant impact' or 'considerable advantage') would show a wider vocabulary.

Some of your word combinations sound natural, such as 'peer pressure' and 'worry about what others think'. Other combinations are less conventional in English. 'Full capability' is usually expressed as 'full potential', and 'is complete fine' would be more natural as 'is completely fine'. Reading widely in academic writing will help you learn which combinations are typical.

There are several agreement and verb-form errors to focus on. Subjects and verbs do not always agree, for example 'rules that needs' and 'The person do not have'. Some verbs are missing the correct form, such as 'to be follow' and 'suppose' (which should be 'supposed'). Also, 'the persons have' should be 'the person has' or 'the persons have' depending on the intended subject. Reviewing subject-verb agreement and verb forms after 'to be' and modal verbs will help.

Your ideas are clear, but spelling and punctuation errors often interrupt the reading. Words such as 'whethere', 'accomplisment', 'becase', and 'no body' need correcting. Possessive apostrophes are missing in phrases such as 'a persons life', and some sentences need capital letters or commas, such as 'because Being able'. Proofreading for these specific patterns, particularly possessives and spelling, would make a noticeable difference.

The conclusion repeats a sentence almost word for word from the third paragraph, so the essay restates points instead of developing them. The two 'however' transitions also switch the position back and forth without a clear line of argument.

The writer does use some complex structures, such as an embedded 'that' clause after 'believe' and a conditional with a relative clause. These are often malformed, which limits control of the structure.
Some content words show promising range, such as 'originality', 'creativity' and 'isolate', which the writer uses in appropriate contexts.

Several collocations are unidiomatic or ungrammatical, such as 'complete fine' (for 'completely fine') and 'bring success into'. Other expressions such as 'worry about what others think' and 'peer pressure' are idiomatic and used correctly.
The writer uses some standard multi-word expressions, such as 'peer pressure' and 'worry about what others think', which show awareness of common phrasing.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear structure: an introduction, three body paragraphs that each develop one idea, and a conclusion that sums up your argument. Transitions such as "For example", "Another reason why" and "In conclusion" guide the reader well. To strengthen cohesion, check the connecting phrases. "in the other hand" should be "on the other hand", and "In overall" should be "Overall". Adding a space after the comma in "do,in the other hand" would also help the reader follow the contrast.

You use a good mix of simple and compound sentences, and some longer sentences join ideas with "if", "because" and "so". To extend your range, try breaking up long chains of clauses joined by "and" or "then". For example, the grandpa sentence could be split into two or three sentences. Using more varied complex structures, such as sentences beginning with subordinate clauses, would also add variety.

You choose clear, mostly appropriate words such as "encounter", "clueless" and "struggling", which show precision. Some words are vague or incorrect in this context. "stuff" is general, "past" should replace "back" in "other people back experiences", and "pick in between" could be more precise. Try to choose words that express your exact meaning, such as "choose between" for the decision idea.

You use several useful collocations correctly, such as "pay close attention", "make a decision", "help them out" and "make the same mistake". Some fixed expressions need correcting: "come handy" should be "come in handy", "in overall" should be "overall", "in the other hand" should be "on the other hand", and "pick in between" is not a standard expression. Learning these set phrases as complete chunks will make your writing sound more natural.

Most of your grammar is accurate, including tense use in the grandpa story and the conditional structures. The main error is confusing "it's" (it is) with "its" (possessive). Also check word forms: "come handy" needs "come in handy". Keep checking your verb and pronoun forms as you write, especially in longer sentences.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but punctuation needs attention. Add commas after introductory words such as "Well", and place commas before clauses such as "then my dad" and "in the other hand", with a space after them. Avoid informal spellings such as "tho" and "Well" at the start of a formal essay. Also use "it's" only for "it is" and "its" for possession. Check your spacing and comma use during editing.

The essay has a clear introduction, two developed reasons, and a conclusion, and it signposts its structure with phrases such as "One of the reasons" and "Another reason". The transition "in the other hand" is misused, which weakens the contrast it is meant to signal.

Most sentences are simple or compound, joined with "and", "so" and "because". Some longer complex sentences appear, such as the conditional with a "because" clause, but the range of structures is narrow and some clauses run together.

The essay uses some appropriate collocations, such as "make a decision" and "make the same mistake". However, "come handy" is a non-standard form of "come in handy", and "in the other hand" is an incorrect fixed expression.

There are several errors in tense and form. "Didn't pay" is followed by the present tense "face" instead of "faced", a possessive is missing its apostrophe, and "smoking it's" is an ungrammatical clause structure.

Punctuation is inconsistent: a comma is missing after "For example" and there is no space after a comma before "then". The informal spelling "tho" appears, and "in the other hand" should read "on the other hand".

Some sentences also repeat the same idea ('the chance' and 'the opportunity' appear several times), which weakens the flow. Using more varied linking words and clearer references back to earlier points would help the reader follow your argument.

You use a good mix of sentence lengths, including longer sentences with several clauses and shorter, direct statements. The main issue is comma splices, where two independent clauses are joined only by a comma. Splitting these into separate sentences or joining them with a conjunction or semicolon would give you more control over your structure.

Other words are vague or general, such as 'a great man,' 'a thing or two,' and 'the wonders of technology,' so the ideas lose some precision. Choosing more specific words that name the skills, qualities, or outcomes you mean would make your writing more persuasive.

You use some effective expressions, such as 'a once in a lifetime thing' and 'the man who started it all,' which sound natural and add personality. The phrase 'followed your footsteps' is a common idiom, but it is normally used with 'in,' so 'followed in your footsteps' would be more idiomatic. Checking verb forms and making sure each sentence has a complete structure will improve your accuracy.

Your punctuation and capitalisation need attention. The possessive 'your companies work' needs an apostrophe ('your company's work'). Also, some sentences are missing commas after introductory phrases, such as 'Ever since then I have been.' Proofreading specifically for capitalisation and apostrophes would make a noticeable difference.

studentFacing: Your essay has a clear overall structure, and you use some transitions to move between examples, such as "Another example was that" and "Last exapmple is that." Some paragraph links are unclear, though. Your opening sentence says you will argue whether students should commit to a career, but your later paragraphs repeat the point that students should think about careers without linking back to the question. Also, the sentence "Most student get into high school without knowing what they would want to study for" appears twice, and the repetition interrupts the flow of your argument. Try adding clearer linking words (for example, "As a result," "For this reason," or "However") and removing repeated points so each paragraph builds on the last.

Most of your sentences follow a simple subject-verb-object pattern, which makes your ideas easy to follow. You do attempt longer sentences, which is a good start. For example, "When i try to get into my step for my second career it was already too late to apply which made me now find my own way to get into the career i wanted to be in" shows you can join ideas. To build range, combine short sentences using subordinate clauses such as "although," "because," or "which," and vary where you place them. Also, try to avoid very long chains of clauses joined by "which" so your meaning stays clear.

You communicate your main ideas, but your word choice is often general or repetitive. Words like "good," "right," "classes," and "get into" appear many times. Try more precise alternatives: for example, instead of "the right one to take" you could write "the most suitable course," and instead of "a rush thing" you could write "a hasty decision." Expanding your range of academic and career-related vocabulary, such as "pursue," "qualifications," "vocational," or "undecided," would make your argument more precise and persuasive.

You use some useful collocations, such as "change my mind" and "find my own way," which sound natural. However, some expressions are not idiomatic in English. "A rush thing" is not a common phrase, and "get into" is used repeatedly where other verbs would be more natural, for example "apply to" a college or "enter" a field. Learning common collocations like "make a decision," "choose a career path," and "apply to university" would help your writing sound more fluent and natural.

Your meaning is usually clear, but there are recurring problems with agreement, tense, and word forms. The noun "student" is often used without a plural ending ("Most student"), and past tense forms are sometimes missing ("they ask me" should be "they asked me"; "i change my mind" should be "I changed my mind"). Also, "i didn't get into any of my career" needs a different noun, such as "any of the careers." Reviewing past simple forms and plural nouns, and checking each sentence for these, will improve your accuracy considerably.

Your ideas are understandable, but several conventions need attention. The pronoun "I" should always be capitalised, and this appears throughout your essay. Some words are misspelled, including "exapmple," "collage" (college), "schoolar" (scholar), and "woukd" (would). "With out" should be written as one word, "without." The title question has a space before the question mark. Proofreading for capitalisation of "I" and common spellings, and checking that your question mark is placed correctly, will make your essay look more polished.

studentFacing: Your ideas are generally in a sensible order: the mother's feedback, then your practice, then the final lesson. To strengthen the links between sentences and paragraphs, add more transitions and reference words such as 'because', 'after that' or 'this is why'. For example, 'it passed two month and then I went to clean again' could show more clearly how your practice led to the improvement.

You use some useful structures, such as 'every time you learn something new' and 'my mom always puts me to clean the house but every time i went to do the cleaning, she used to say'. Most sentences are short or joined with 'and' or 'so'. Try combining ideas using more varied subordinate clauses, such as 'Although she criticised me, I kept trying', to show more control over sentence structure.

You communicate your story clearly with words such as 'clean', 'mop', 'windows' and 'tables'. 'Clean' is repeated many times, so try synonyms or more precise verbs, such as 'scrub', 'tidy' or 'sweep', to make your word choice more varied and exact.

Your text contains some good expressions, such as 'keep working on it' and 'keep dreaming'. Some phrases sound unnatural in English, for example 'in a perfect way' (you could say 'perfectly') and 'i keep smiling not given up' (you could say 'I keep smiling and never give up'). Learning common collocations like 'give up' and 'do well' will help your writing sound more natural.

Your writing communicates clearly, but several grammar points need attention. Use the base form after 'you' ('you fail', not 'you failure'), the past tense of 'do' ('didn't', not 'din't'), the plural 'months', and a past form of 'mop' ('I mopped'). Also keep your tenses consistent, and use 'I'm going to' rather than 'gonna' in formal writing. Finally, 'to succeed' is the correct form, not 'to success'.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but punctuation and capitalisation need work. Write 'I' with a capital letter every time, place commas directly after words rather than before them, and use a single full stop or exclamation mark rather than repeated marks. Some sentences are harder to follow, though. The sentence "It does not mean that others are smart." is unclear because "It" has no clear referent, and the list of activities in your second paragraph would read more smoothly if you linked the ideas to each other. Adding more explicit connectors between sentences, and making sure each pronoun clearly refers to a noun, would help the reader follow your reasoning.

You use a range of structures, including conditional and purpose clauses such as "if some student are good in a activity" and "so they all can help each other." Some sentences are fragments or run-ons, however, such as "And learn how to work with others." and "Extending school it will help them get their grades up,". Joining these with full clauses or using a conjunction would give your sentences more control. You also begin many sentences with "Also" and "And", so varying your openings would show more range.

You use some useful academic words, such as "opportunity," "conclusion," and "benefit," and you choose a fitting term in "explained what they are good at." Several words are repeated or imprecise, however. "A lot of" and "get more" appear many times, and "motive" should be "motivate." Choosing more specific verbs and a wider range of words for ideas like improvement and participation would make your meaning sharper.

You use some strong collocations, such as "get their grades up," "learn new skills," and "get to a conclusion." Some common word combinations are not used idiomatically, though. People say "take a vote" rather than "make a vote," "a large percentage of students" rather than "a big percent of student," and "by themselves" rather than "by them self." The phrase "do another period" also sounds unnatural. Learning standard collocations for school contexts would make your writing sound more natural.

Your grammar shows good control of modal verbs like "will" and "can" in your predictions. There are recurring errors, though. "Student" is often used without a plural "s" where a plural is needed, the verb "used" appears after "can" instead of "use," and the word "explained" should be "explain" after "and." Subject-verb agreement also needs attention, as in "some student needs help" and "school board add." Reviewing plural nouns, base verbs after modals, and third-person agreement would help your accuracy.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but punctuation and spelling need attention. Many sentences need a space after the comma or period, and some sentences run together without punctuation between clauses. Some words are misspelled or used incorrectly, such as "there" for "their" in "passing there SOL." Lowercase "student" is used throughout where it should be capitalised at the start of sentences, and "Math,English,civic" needs spaces and capitals for the subjects. Careful proofreading would make the essay look more polished.

studentFacing: Your ideas are connected by repeating the key topic (students, careers, goals), which helps the reader follow the main point. To strengthen cohesion, use more linking words such as 'because,' 'however,' or 'for example' between sentences, and make sure each paragraph clearly supports your claim. The counterargument paragraph would be easier to follow with a clear transition showing that you are responding to the opposing view.

You use simple and compound sentences joined by 'and' correctly. Try varying your sentence structures by using subordinate clauses (such as 'when,' 'because,' or 'although') and by breaking up long chains of clauses. Some sentences in the examples run on for a long time, so dividing them would make your meaning clearer.

You use some useful topic words such as 'career,' 'achievement,' and 'goal.' Watch for word-form and meaning accuracy: 'achiever' is a person, while 'achievement' is the thing reached, so check which one fits the sentence. Also, 'things' and 'good way' are used many times; try more specific words like 'skills,' 'experience,' or 'opportunities' to express your ideas more precisely.

You use the common expression 'reach their goals' correctly, which is a strong collocation. Some other expressions are not yet standard in English, such as 'get good safe' and 'put them in a good way.' Learning common phrases such as 'in a safe position,' 'put them on the right path,' or 'achieve their goals' would make your writing sound more natural.

Your writing shows a good understanding of how to express ideas, but there are regular issues with subject-verb agreement and verb forms. For example, use 'were' with plural subjects like 'many people,' and use the past tense 'got' instead of 'get' when describing past events. Also use the correct form of 'be' and the base form after modal verbs such as 'should' and 'can' (for example, 'can teach' rather than 'can teaching'). Using 'she' or 'they' as subjects and 'her' or 'them' as objects will also help.

Your sentences begin with capital letters and you use commas to separate ideas, which is good. Work on spelling, especially words like 'because,' 'student,' 'studrents,' 'believe,' and 'conclusion,' and check that headings like 'Counterclaim' and 'Conclusion' are spelled correctly. Also add missing spaces after commas and use apostrophes correctly, as in 'it's' for 'it is' versus 'its' for possession.

The essay relies on few explicit transitions. The one logical connector, "Therefore:", is followed by a claim that does not clearly follow from the rebuttal before it. The rebuttal paragraph also begins with a malformed label, so the link between the counterargument and the writer's position is hard to follow.
The writer uses some subordinate clauses ("who", "because", "when"), which shows some range. Control is inconsistent, though, and most sentences are short or coordinated with "and".
Word choice is limited and sometimes imprecise. "trust" and "believe" are used repeatedly as general-purpose verbs, and "an achiever" is used where a different word is needed.

Phrases are generic and sometimes non-idiomatic, such as "in a good way" and "get a good safe in their life". Standard collocations like "reach their goals" appear, but the expression is repetitive and often unidiomatic.
Errors are frequent and affect agreement, tense and word forms, including omitted articles and prepositions, wrong past-tense forms, and verb forms after modal and auxiliary structures.

studentFacing: Your paragraphs follow a clear order: your goal, why Mexico, how practice leads to games, championships, and the World Cup. Transitions such as "Sometimes we don't just play friendly games" and "Sometimes we play in leagues" help the reader follow the sequence. However, you switch between "I" and "we" without a clear reason, and some references are unclear. For example, "I am representing myself and to the people in Mexico" does not make it clear who you are representing. Use one consistent point of view and make sure each pronoun has a clear referent.

Most of your sentences are simple or joined with "and" or "but." You do use some longer structures well, such as "We play to learn so that if we lose we get to see where we made our mistakes." Try combining more short sentences using subordinate clauses (because, although, when, which) to show a wider range of sentence structures.

You use the topic words "tactics," "strategies," "qualify," and "knock out stages" accurately, which shows good subject knowledge. However, "play" and "good" are repeated many times, and the list "play,train,play championships" uses "play" again instead of a more precise verb. Look for more specific verbs and adjectives to replace repeated words. Also check the spelling of "inffiencetly," which should be "efficiently."

You use several useful expressions, such as "work very hard," "try our best to win," and "get knocked out of the championship," which sound natural in this context. Expanding your range of collocations, such as "go through to the next round" or "reach the final," would make your writing sound more fluent and idiomatic.

Your sentences are mostly grammatical, and verb tenses are generally consistent. There is a subject-verb agreement error in "Friendly games is a game of fun." The plural subject "Friendly games" needs "are." Also check word forms, since "learning it" should be "learning them" or "learning about it" depending on your meaning, and "We have to be first in the stage" would read more naturally as "We have to be first in the stage to win the trophies." Reread each sentence to check agreement and word forms.

Your capitalization of "Mexico" and "World Cup" is correct. However, there are several spelling and punctuation errors. "inffiencetly" should be "efficiently," "play,train,play" needs spaces after the commas, and "knock out stages" is usually written as "knockout stages." Proofread for spelling and spacing, and add a comma before "but" in longer compound sentences.

The essay moves through practice, friendly games, championships and the World Cup in a clear sequence, and some sentences signal the order, such as 'After practice'. However, paragraphs often open with unconnected statements and rely on repeated 'we' rather than linking words, so the logical relations between ideas (e.g., why friendly games matter for improvement) are left implicit.

The writer uses some complex structures, including a conditional with a contrasting clause and a purpose clause with a nested 'if' clause, but most sentences are simple or joined with 'and'. The range is therefore limited, though the complex sentences are mostly controlled.

The writer uses some topic-specific words such as 'tactics', 'strategies' and 'qualify', but much of the vocabulary is basic and repetitive ('play', 'fun', 'good', 'get'). The misspelled 'inffiencetly' also obscures an intended word, which reduces precision.

Some collocations are natural ('work hard', 'try our best'), but others are non-standard, such as 'knock out stages' (usually 'knockout stages') and 'get into games'. Idiomatic multi-word expressions are largely absent beyond these few.

Several grammar errors occur: subject-verb agreement ('Friendly games is'), an incorrect word form ('inffiencetly' for 'efficiently', which is also a spelling issue), and a broken structure ('is a part of championship wise'). Tense and most agreement are otherwise controlled, so meaning is usually clear despite the errors.

Spelling errors are frequent in key words, including 'inffiencetly' and 'knock out' written as two words. Capitalisation is generally correct, but a comma is missing after the opening conditional clause, and the sentence about representing a country is hard to parse.

Your ideas generally follow a clear order: an introduction, a Ronaldo example, a personal example, and a conclusion. Linking words such as "Hard work made him" and "As you can see" help signal your reasoning. The transition between the Ronaldo and mom paragraphs is abrupt, though, and a connector such as "Another example" or "A closer example" would help. Pronouns sometimes refer back unclearly, so check that each one clearly points to its noun.

You use a mix of short and longer sentences, and some of your sentences include subordinate clauses, such as "When people have the type motivation fail is just a symple word..." To build on this, try joining more ideas with varied structures. Some run-on sentences, such as the one about your mom, would read more clearly if split or joined with a connector.

You use some useful topic words, such as "enthusiasm," "motivation," and "failure," and you define "enthusiasm" in your own words. Some word choices are imprecise or misspelled, such as "impulsed" (which should be "impelled" or "pushed") and "loss" (which should be "lost"). Using more precise verbs and adjectives would make your ideas stronger.

You use several useful expressions, such as "never give up," "get up," "keep trying," and "keep working hard." The phrase "Enthusiasm made him work harder and harder" is a natural collocation. Adding a few more idiomatic expressions, such as "bounce back" or "stay the course," would make your writing sound more fluent.

Your writing shows several recurring grammar issues. Check verb forms after auxiliaries ("had to took" should be "had to take"; "did not tooked" should be "did not take"). Check past tense ("she toked" and "she fail" should be "took" and "failed"). Check subject-verb agreement ("he fail" and "Fail mades people"). Check word forms ("succes" for "success," "succesfully" for "successfully"). Pay attention to these patterns in your next draft; they are the most important focus for improvement.

Your writing has frequent spelling errors, such as "Succes," "somethig," "specally," "enthusiams," "foward," and "Licence" (for the Driver Licence). Capitalisation is inconsistent, as in "soccer playes" and the word "Driver Licence." Punctuation also needs attention: there are spaces before commas ("example ,") and commas are missing after introductory clauses ("When he begins his soccer correar ,he was seen"). Proofreading for these errors would make your essay much easier to read.

studentFacing: Your ideas connect well in places. The sentence "By helping people in the hospital, you can help people that are sick" clearly links back to the hospital example. Try adding more transitions like "For example" and "Also" to show how each idea builds on the last. Your last paragraph about the principal starts a new idea, so a clearer link to your main point would help the reader follow your argument.

You use a variety of sentence openings, such as the introductory phrase "By helping people in the hospital," which is a good choice. Most of your sentences follow a similar pattern, often joined with "and." Try combining short sentences and using subordinate clauses (for example, "because," "although," or "when") to add variety and show more control over sentence structure.

You choose clear, everyday words such as "tutor," "litter," and "decide," which fit the topic. However, "help" and "helpful" are repeated many times. Try replacing some of them with more specific words, such as "assist," "support," "benefit," or "improve," to make your writing more precise.

You use a useful collocation with "clean up litter." Some expressions are less natural, however. "clean up from the parks and the street floor" is hard to understand, and "got a 75% or higher" is more often phrased as "earned" or "received" a grade. Learning common phrases such as "clean up after," "pick up litter," or "receive a grade of" will help your writing sound more natural.

Your verb forms are mostly correct and consistent. Check your prepositions and pronouns. "clean up from the parks" should be "clean up the parks" or "clean up in the parks." Also, when referring to people, use "who" instead of "that" (for example, "the people who got"). Reviewing these points will make your sentences more accurate.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but there are several punctuation and capitalisation issues. Use a capital "I" every time you write the pronoun (for example, "I think" instead of "i think"). The greeting has stray quotation marks, and "Dear principal" should be followed by a comma and capitalised as "Principal" if used as a title. Add a comma after introductory phrases such as "For example" and "By helping people in the hospital."

studentFacing: Your essay is organised into separate paragraphs, and you use some linking words such as 'In adition' and 'Even'. However, the first paragraph about your uncle's spending is not clearly connected to the question about seeking multiple opinions, so the reader has to work out the link. Try opening each paragraph with a sentence that states its main point, and use linking words more consistently to show how each example supports your argument.

Most of your sentences are simple or joined with 'and' and 'but'. Some sentences run together without punctuation, which makes them hard to follow. Practise separating long ideas into clear sentences, and try using subordinate clauses such as 'because', 'although' or 'when' to show relationships between ideas.

You use some good content words, such as 'obsession' and 'perspective', which show you can express ideas precisely. Other word choices are not quite right or are misspelled, which can confuse the reader. Keep a list of words you want to use and check their meaning and spelling before you write.

You have some natural expressions, such as 'spend all the money' and 'stay with the rest'. However, several set phrases and collocations are not used in their standard forms, such as 'Once of my friend' and 'the case that happen in resume'. Learning common phrases as whole chunks, such as 'one of my friends' and 'in summary', will help your writing sound more natural.

Your essay shows that you understand the ideas you want to express, but there are frequent errors with verb forms and subject-verb agreement. For example, third-person verbs need an 's' ending, and past tense forms are often missing or incorrect. Reviewing present simple and past simple forms, and checking each verb as you finish a sentence, will make a big difference to your accuracy.

Your writing has several spelling mistakes, including 'whatch', 'recibe', 'nezt' and 'spended'. Capital letters are often missing, such as the pronoun 'i' and the first word of some sentences. Sentences are sometimes joined with commas where a full stop or semicolon is needed. Proofreading for these three areas will improve your score quickly.

Ideas connect mainly through repeated topic words rather than clear logical links. The uncle anecdote, the friend anecdote and the father anecdote are separated by abrupt shifts, and the closing question to the reader is not tied to the preceding argument.

Most sentences are simple or joined by 'and' or 'but'. One long sentence chains several clauses with commas and a misplaced appositive ending, so the structure becomes hard to follow, and there is little use of subordination to show relations between ideas.

Vocabulary is mostly everyday and generally adequate for the topic. Some word choices are imprecise or misspelled ('choise', 'paket', 'recibe'), and some terms are vague or used loosely, which limits precision.

Collocations are often unidiomatic, such as 'spend all the money' with the wrong verb form, 'buy things with the money', and 'we was need it'. Few fixed or multi-word expressions appear, so the phrasing sounds literal rather than idiomatic.

Errors recur across the piece: verb tense and form ('he give', 'he spended', 'was asking' used inconsistently), subject-verb agreement ('there were listen'), and auxiliary use ('i did't listen'). These errors appear frequently enough to affect clarity.

Spelling errors ('choise', 'recibe', 'whatch', 'nezt'), missing spaces after commas, and lowercase 'i' appear throughout. Capitalisation of 'In' mid-sentence and missing apostrophes/letters add to the inconsistency.

studentFacing: Your ideas about asking others for help are clear in places, and you link some points with "Then" and "And." However, the paragraphs don't always connect well. The heading "Tone- expiring" doesn't match the paragraph below it, and "Therefor" starts a new idea without clearly following from the paragraph before. Try using clearer transitions such as "For example," "As a result," or "In addition," and make sure each paragraph's heading and topic sentence match its content.

Most of your sentences are short and simple, and some are joined with "and." Some longer sentences run together several ideas without clear punctuation, which makes them hard to follow. Practise joining ideas with subordinating conjunctions such as "because," "when," or "although," and break up very long sentences into two or more clear ones.

You use some useful words, such as "smarter," "options," and "details." Some word choices are not quite right, though. "Hunted house" should be "haunted house," and "advice" is used where you need a countable noun in some places. Check spelling and meaning in your word choices, and use a dictionary or thesaurus to find more precise words.

You use some common expressions correctly, such as "come up with," "make a better choice," and "in a good way." Other word combinations sound unnatural, such as "every one will many ideas," which would be clearer as "everyone will have many ideas." Learning and practising common collocations will make your writing sound more natural.

There are several errors with word forms and verb use. "Your" is used where "you're" is needed, "you cant" needs an apostrophe, and "a idea" should be "an idea." Also check verb forms, such as "your doing" (you're doing) and "you were writing" (you were writing a main idea). Reviewing these patterns will help your sentences become more accurate.

Several sentences start with lowercase letters, and some are missing spaces after punctuation, for example "ideas,something." Apostrophes are missing in words such as "cant," and "Therefor" should be "Therefore." Checking capital letters at the start of sentences, spacing after commas, and apostrophes will make your writing easier to read.

Paragraphs follow one another without a clear overall line of argument, and the headings ('Manner-better choices', 'Tone- expiring') do not match the content beneath them. Transitions are mostly repeated 'Then' and 'Therefor' connectors, which show sequence but not logical relationships between ideas.

Most sentences are simple or run-on, with clauses joined by 'and' and 'if'. A complex sentence about group ideas is garbled and missing a verb, and some sentences are fragments or unclear, so the range of structures is narrow and control is inconsistent.

studentFacing: Your ideas follow a clear order: you state a position, add a counterpoint, give a second argument, and end with a conclusion. Linking words such as "But" and "also" help signal these moves. To improve, use a wider range of connectors (for example, "however," "for example," "as a result") and check that words like "because" and "even though" connect the ideas you intend. Some links are unclear, such as "Even thought in school you can't keep failing," which does not clearly connect to the paragraph's argument.

You use a mix of sentence types, including a few longer sentences with several linked clauses, such as the one about failing and getting bored. Many sentences, however, are long chains joined by "and" or "because" without punctuation, which makes them hard to follow. Try breaking some of them into shorter sentences, and practise using commas and subordinate clauses to control how ideas are combined.

You use some appropriate words, such as "consists of" and "Churchill's statement," which show you are trying to write in an academic register. Much of your vocabulary is general or repeated ("life," "success," "fail"), and some words are used in forms that do not fit the meaning, such as "success" used as a verb. Try using more precise alternatives, such as "achieve," "succeed," "setback," or "persevere," to express your ideas more exactly.

Some of your expressions are understandable but do not sound natural in English, such as "you can't just success in life" and "no one in life have success." Standard collocations would be "achieve success," "be successful," or "succeed in life." Phrases like "going from failure to failure" are also unusual. Learning common fixed expressions about failure and perseverance, such as "learn from your mistakes" or "keep trying," would make your writing sound more fluent.

Your writing contains several errors in word forms, agreement and tense. For example, "success" is used where a verb or a different noun form is needed ("to be success," "did not success"), and subject-verb agreement is inconsistent ("no one in life have"). Focus on the forms of verbs and nouns (succeed/success/successful) and on matching subjects with verbs. Checking your sentences for these points after drafting will help a lot.

Many common words are misspelled, including "Bacuse," "fialling," "becuase," "disagrer," "comclusion," "leasd," and "evry." Punctuation also needs attention: there is no space after the comma in "job,place," and the word "i" should be capitalised. Proofreading for spelling and checking a list of frequently misspelled words, such as "because," "success," and "every," would make a clear improvement.

studentFacing: You use signposting phrases such as "For example" to introduce your personal stories, which helps the reader follow your reasoning. Transitions like "In the other hand" and "In a other hand" are not quite right, though. "On the other hand" is the standard form, and it signals a contrast to the idea before it. Your paragraphs also each stay with one main idea, which makes the essay easy to follow.

Most of your sentences are simple or compound, which makes your meaning clear. You also attempt some longer, more complex sentences with multiple clauses, such as the one about a good attitude and learning from others. Try combining more of your short sentences using subordinate clauses (because, although, when, which) to add variety and show more control over sentence structure.

You choose clear, everyday words that get your message across. To extend your range, look for more precise alternatives. For example, "positively words" could be "encouraging words" and "nigtivety" should be "negativity". Also, try stronger words in place of general ones like "good" and "bad" to make your ideas more vivid.

You use some useful expressions, such as "make new friends" and "have a hard time", which sound natural. Some phrases need correcting, though. "Take to" should be "talk to", and "made me in a good attitude" would be more natural as "put me in a good mood" or "made me feel positive". Learning common collocations like these will make your writing sound more fluent.

Several verb forms and subject-verb agreements need attention. Use third-person forms with singular subjects (for example, "attitude makes" rather than "attitude make"). Use the past simple "saw" rather than "seen" after "we", and check which word form is needed in each sentence ("people out who had" should probably be "people who have had" or "people who have"). Reviewing these patterns will help your sentences become more accurate.

Your ideas are easy to follow, but there are frequent errors in punctuation and capitalisation. Write "I" with a capital letter every time, add apostrophes in contractions ("can't", "don't"), and put a space after commas. Also check spellings such as "road" (not "rode") and "brother" (not "bother"). Reading your work aloud and proofreading for these points will improve it noticeably.
